title: Doubles, Bunny Chow, and Nasi Kandar: Inside Drāvida, the East Village Restaurant Tracing South Asia's Diaspora Through Food
excerpt: Chef Aarthi Sampath's new Manhattan restaurant maps the migration of South Asian flavours from Trinidad to Guyana to South Africa — one plate at a time.
body:
When Aarthi Sampath wrote the concept for Drāvida in 2019, she was not thinking about another Indian restaurant in New York. She was thinking about the millions of South Asians whose kitchens are scattered across continents — from the chutney-drenched doubles stands of Port of Spain to the bunny chow vendors of Durban — and whose food has rarely had a seat at the fine-dining table.

Now, seven years later, that concept has opened its doors at 211 1st Avenue in Manhattan's East Village. And for a growing number of New Yorkers in the diaspora, it feels like something overdue.

## A Menu That Moves With Migration

Drāvida — the name nods to the Dravidian cultures of southern India — traces the movement of South Asian flavours across regions and generations. The menu spans the cuisines of India, Sri Lanka, Pakistan, Nepal, Trinidad, Guyana, Indonesia, Malaysia, and South Africa, drawing on the communities that carried their recipes across oceans during and after the colonial era.

The result is a menu that reads like a geography lesson in the best possible way. Highlights include Doubles, the beloved Trinidadian street snack of fried bara bread and curried chickpeas that anchors the street food scene across the Caribbean. There is Oxtail Bunny Chow, the South African favourite served in a hollowed-out loaf of bread, a dish born in Durban's Indian community. The Idli & Shrimp merges South Indian comfort with Indonesian influences. And the Nasi Kandar Feast — a hearty Indo-Malay spread of rice, curries, and accompaniments — nods to the Tamil Muslim communities of Penang.

"This restaurant is for New Yorkers who haven't seen their food represented — for the communities that built this city and whose cuisines haven't always had a place at the table," Sampath said in a statement.

## From Chopped Champion to Diaspora Storyteller

Sampath, who grew up in a Tamilian family in Mumbai, trained at the Taj group before moving to the United States in 2012. She studied at Johnson & Wales University, worked under Vikas Khanna at Junoon, and in 2016 became the first Indian chef to win the American reality cooking show Chopped. She later helmed the kitchen at the Rainbow Room at Rockefeller Center and served as a judge on MasterChef Tamil.

But Drāvida represents a more personal ambition. Sampath has long resisted labels like "modern Indian chef," arguing that they flatten the extraordinary diversity of South Asian foodways. The new restaurant is her attempt to expand the frame entirely — to show that Indian food is not just butter chicken and biryani, but a global story of migration, adaptation, and reinvention.

## The Cocktail Programme Matches the Ambition

Complementing the food is a cocktail programme that reimagines familiar South Asian flavours. The menu includes a tropical Passionfruit Lassi, a floral, citrus-forward Dravida Highball, and the indulgent Orange Cream, inspired by nostalgic dessert flavours that echo childhood treats across the subcontinent.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs and second-generation South Asians in New York, Drāvida arrives at a moment when the city's Indian dining scene is experiencing an unprecedented renaissance. Dishoom is expected to open later this year. Sujan Sarkar's Indienne recently launched in Hudson Yards. And three Indian chefs — Vijaya Kumar, Chetan Shetty, and Sujan Sarkar — now hold Michelin stars in New York, Washington DC, and Chicago respectively.

But Drāvida occupies a different lane. It is not fine-dining Indian or fast-casual Indian. It is a restaurant that asks a bigger question: what happens to food when people move? For the Indo-Trinidadian in Jackson Heights, the Sri Lankan Tamil in Staten Island, or the South African Indian in Jersey City, Sampath is cooking their answer.

Drāvida is now open for dinner service in the East Village. Reservations are available through the restaurant's website.
